teile.einleitung: Internally displaced people are people who had to leave their homes but have stayed in their own country. The reasons are wars, violence or natural disasters. At the end of 2024 there were more internally displaced people than ever before.
wichtigste: Internally displaced people have not crossed an international border.
That is why the Geneva Refugee Convention does not apply to them.
At the end of 2024 there were around 83 million internally displaced people according to the IDMC.
The main causes are conflict and violence as well as disasters.
Their own state is mainly responsible for their protection.
At the end of 2024 Sudan had the most people displaced by conflict.

abschnitte.text: **Refugees** in the sense of the **Geneva Refugee Convention** have left their country and crossed a border. **Internally displaced people** also had to flee but stayed in their own country. That is why the Refugee Convention does not apply to them. Under international law, the **state itself** bears the main responsibility for their protection. International organisations only help in addition.

The **Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre** (IDMC) collects worldwide figures every year. It was founded in 1998 by the Norwegian Refugee Council and is based in **Geneva**. At the end of 2024 it counted around **83.4 million** internally displaced people, for the first time over 80 million. The statistics distinguish two main causes: **conflict and violence** and **disasters** such as floods or cyclones. Displacement by conflict often lasts many years.

In **Sudan** a war broke out in 2023. At the end of 2024 around **11.6 million** people there were displaced within the country. That is the highest number ever recorded for a single country. Many people live in camps or with relatives and need water, food and medical help. But aid organisations do not always get **access** to them.

In 1998 the UN published the **Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement**. They bring together existing human rights for internally displaced people. They are not binding but are widely recognised internationally. In 2009 the **African Union** adopted the **Kampala Convention**, the first regionally binding agreement specifically for internally displaced people. It came into force in 2012. Protection remains difficult when the government itself is a party to the conflict.

gewusst: Worldwide there are clearly more internally displaced people than refugees who have left their country.
The IDMC’s annual report is called the “Global Report on Internal Displacement”.

teile.einleitung: Bhutan is a small kingdom in the Himalayas between India and China. The country is known for its monasteries, its forests and a special idea: Gross National Happiness. The capital is called Thimphu.
wichtigste: Bhutan lies between India and China and has no access to the sea.
The capital is Thimphu, and the international airport is in Paro.
Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy with a constitution since 2008.
Besides the economy, Bhutan measures Gross National Happiness.
The currency is called the ngultrum.
According to the constitution, at least 60 per cent of the country must be forested.

abschnitte.text: **Bhutan** borders China (Tibet) in the north and **India** otherwise. The country has no access to the sea. In the north rise high mountains of the **Himalayas**, and in the south it is lower and warmer. The capital and largest city is **Thimphu**. The international airport lies in the nearby valley of **Paro**. People pay with the **ngultrum**, which is worth the same as the Indian rupee.

Bhutan is a **constitutional monarchy**. That means there is a king, but since 2008 his power has been limited by a **constitution**. The people elect a **parliament**. The change to democracy came from the king himself. Most people in Bhutan are **Buddhists**, and Buddhist culture shapes the whole country.

Many countries measure their success mainly by **economic output**. Bhutan also measures **Gross National Happiness**. This includes well-being, health, education, culture and an intact environment. The idea comes from the fourth king, **Jigme Singye Wangchuck**. It is meant to show that money alone does not make people happy.

The **constitution** requires that at least **60 per cent** of the country stay covered with forest. In fact, today even more of the area is forested. Famous are the many **monasteries** and fortresses, which are called **dzongs**. The best-known monastery is **Taktsang**, the “Tiger’s Nest”. It clings high above the Paro Valley to a steep rock wall and is one of Bhutan’s landmarks.

gewusst: In the national language Bhutan is called “Druk Yul”, which means “Land of the Thunder Dragon”.
Switzerland has supported Bhutan for decades with development cooperation, for example through the aid organisation Helvetas.

teile.einleitung: A caldera is a large basin that forms at a volcano. It forms when, after a huge eruption, the roof above the emptied magma chamber collapses. Many calderas are filled with water today.
wichtigste: “Caldera” comes from Spanish and Portuguese and means cauldron.
A caldera forms by collapse above an emptied magma chamber.
It is much bigger than an ordinary volcanic crater.
Crater Lake in Oregon fills the caldera of Mount Mazama.
The island of Santorini surrounds a caldera flooded by the sea.
In 2018, the summit caldera of Kīlauea in Hawaii sank in stages.

abschnitte.text: Beneath a volcano lies a **magma chamber** with molten rock. In a very large eruption it is partly emptied. The rock above then loses its **support**. It collapses, and a huge **basin** forms. It is much bigger than an ordinary **crater**. The word caldera means “cauldron”. The geologist **Leopold von Buch** took it from the **Caldera de Taburiente** on La Palma.

Many calderas fill with water. About **7,700 years ago**, **Mount Mazama** in Oregon erupted and collapsed. Rain and snow filled the caldera to make **Crater Lake**, which is nearly 600 metres deep. On Sumatra, **Lake Toba** fills the caldera of a supervolcano that erupted about 74,000 years ago. Later, magma lifted the ground, creating the island of **Samosir**. In the German **Eifel**, the **Laacher See** lies in a caldera that formed about 13,000 years ago.

The Greek island of **Santorini** surrounds a caldera that is **flooded by the sea**. It formed in the **Minoan eruption** around 1600 BC. This eruption was one of the largest of the last 10,000 years. The steep rock walls at the edge now form the backdrop for the island’s white villages. Ships sail right into the middle of the old caldera.

In **Tanzania** lies the **Ngorongoro Crater**. It is really a large, well-preserved caldera about **20 kilometres** across. The volcano is extinct. On the floor of the caldera live many **large animals**, for example zebras, wildebeest, lions and elephants. The area is a well-known **nature reserve**.

Some calderas are still active. In the **Phlegraean Fields** near Naples, the ground rises and falls again and again by metres. This is called **bradyseism**, “slow quaking”. In Hawaii in **2018**, lava emerged far away in **Puna** from **Kīlauea**. Because the magma beneath the summit drained away sideways, the **summit caldera sank** by hundreds of metres in many stages. Experts were able to watch a caldera form live.

gewusst: Yellowstone National Park in the USA also contains a huge caldera.
The ash from the Laacher See eruption is used by researchers as a time marker in old lake deposits.

teile.einleitung: Dakar is the capital of the West African country of Senegal. The city lies on the Atlantic on a peninsula that juts far out into the sea. Dakar is an important port and a centre of culture and trade.
wichtigste: Dakar is the capital of Senegal.
The city lies on the Cap-Vert peninsula on the Atlantic.
The westernmost point of the African mainland is here.
Dakar has a large sea port.
Off the city lies the island of Gorée, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
In 2010 the African Renaissance Monument was inaugurated.

abschnitte.titel: In the far west of Africa
abschnitte.text: Dakar lies on the **Cap-Vert** peninsula, which means “green cape”. Here is the **westernmost point** of the African mainland. Senegal was a French colony for a long time and became independent in **1960**. The official language is French, and in everyday life many people speak **Wolof**.

Because of its position on the **Atlantic**, Dakar has a large **sea port**. Ships bring goods from all over the world, and peanuts, fish and other goods are shipped from here. Landlocked countries such as Mali also use the port. In the past, Dakar was the capital of all **French West Africa**.

Off Dakar lies the small island of **Gorée**. It recalls the **slave trade**, in which millions of people were forcibly taken from Africa to the Americas. The well-known “House of Slaves” is now a museum. Since 1978 Gorée has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and a place of remembrance.

In 2010, the **African Renaissance Monument** was inaugurated on a hill. The bronze figure shows a man, a woman and a child looking forward. At about 49 metres, it is taller than the Statue of Liberty in New York. The monument is meant to show Africa’s new beginning, but was also controversial because of its high cost.

gewusst: For many years Dakar was the destination of the famous Paris-Dakar car rally.
The African Renaissance Monument is one of the tallest statues in Africa.

teile.einleitung: A barchan is a dune in the shape of a sickle or crescent. Barchans form in deserts where the wind always blows from the same direction and there is only a little sand. They slowly migrate across the ground.
wichtigste: A barchan is a sickle-shaped or crescent-shaped dune.
Its two tips are called horns and point in the wind direction.
The windward side is flat, the leeward side steep at about 30 to 35 degrees.
Barchans form with one wind direction and little sand.
Small barchans migrate faster than large ones.
Sand moves mainly by jumping, which is called saltation.

abschnitte.titel: A dune like a crescent moon
abschnitte.text: From above a **barchan** looks like a sickle. Its two tips are called **horns**. They point in the direction in which the wind blows, that is, **downwind**. This is because the sand at the low edges moves faster than in the higher centre. So the horns race ahead.

The side the wind comes from is called the **windward** side. There the barchan is **flat**, and the wind drives the sand up it. The opposite side is called the **leeward** side. There the sand slides off and forms a steep **slip face**. Dry sand can only lie at a certain angle, the **angle of repose**. It is about 30 to 35 degrees.

Barchans form preferably on **firm ground** where only **a little sand** lies and the wind blows steadily from **one direction**. If there is a lot of sand, long **transverse dunes** tend to form. With changing winds **star dunes** with several arms form. In the **parabolic dune** the arms point into the wind, because plants hold them in place while the middle part keeps moving.

A dune migrates as the wind carries sand from the windward side over the crest onto the leeward side. Most of the grains jump in flat arcs across the ground. This **saltation** usually happens only a few decimetres above the ground. **Small barchans** migrate faster than large ones, because less sand has to be moved. Some barchans move several metres a year in this way.

gewusst: Space probes have also photographed dunes in barchan form on Mars.
Migrating dunes can cover roads and fields in the desert.

teile.einleitung: Boleadoras, or bolas, are an ancient throwing weapon from South America. They consist of balls fixed to cords. They are best known as a tool of the gauchos, the cattle herders of the pampas.
wichtigste: Bolas consist of two or three balls on cords.
The cords are usually made of leather, and the balls are often stones covered in leather.
The gauchos used them to catch animals without killing them.
When thrown, the cords wrap around an animal’s legs.
The native peoples of South America used bolas long before the Europeans arrived.

abschnitte.text: Bolas consist of **two or three balls** hanging from long cords. The cords are joined together in the middle. The thrower swings the balls over their head and then lets go. In flight they spin, and when they hit an animal’s legs, **the cords wrap around them**. The animal stumbles and can no longer run away.

The **gauchos** were mounted cattle herders on the **pampas**, the wide grasslands of Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil. With bolas they caught cattle, horses and wild animals such as the **rhea**, a large flightless bird. The name comes from the Spanish word “bola”, which means “ball”. Today bolas are a symbol of gaucho culture and are often shown at festivals.

Bolas were not invented by the gauchos. The **native peoples of South America** hunted with them long before Europeans came to the land. Archaeologists have found old, worked **stone balls** in many places that were used for this. The gauchos took over the weapon and made it famous.

gewusst: A skilled thrower can hit a running animal from a long way away.
Because the animals were only tied up, they could be caught alive.

teile.einleitung: Population density shows how closely people live together in an area. It is given in inhabitants per square kilometre. On Earth it is distributed very unevenly.
wichtigste: Population density means inhabitants per square kilometre.
You calculate number of inhabitants divided by area.
Monaco is the most densely populated state in the world.
Mongolia is the most thinly populated state.
Bangladesh is the larger country with the highest density.
In Switzerland Basel-Stadt has the highest density.

abschnitte.text: **Population density** states how many people on average live on one **square kilometre**. You divide the **number of inhabitants by the area**. You can also calculate the other way round: if a town has 120,000 inhabitants and a density of 4,000 per km², you divide 120,000 by 4,000 and get an area of 30 km². If an island is 50 km² in size and has 300 inhabitants per km², then 300 times 50, so 15,000 people, live there.

The most densely populated is the city-state of **Monaco**. On around 2 km² live almost 40,000 people, which gives almost 20,000 inhabitants per km². Among the larger states, **Bangladesh** with over 1,000 inhabitants per km² is especially densely populated. It is about three and a half times the size of Switzerland but has around 175 million inhabitants. Many people in a small space are found above all in **cities** and fertile river valleys.

The most thinly populated is **Mongolia**. Only around 2 people per km² live there, because large parts of the country are **steppe and desert**. In **Australia**, too, the interior, the **Outback**, is very dry. That is why most Australians live in the coastal cities. In **Egypt** over 90 per cent of the area is desert. Almost all people live in the **Nile Valley and the Nile Delta**, where the river brings water.

Switzerland has around 9 million inhabitants on around 41,000 km², which is about **220 inhabitants per km²**. But people are distributed unevenly. In the **Central Plateau** and in the cities many live, in the Alps few. The canton of **Basel-Stadt** is very small and consists almost entirely of urban area. There live over 5,000 people per km², more than in any other canton.

gewusst: Density is only an average: even in a densely populated country there can be almost empty areas.
Large parts of the Swiss Alps are hardly habitable because of rock, ice and steep slopes.

teile.einleitung: The blue-footed booby is a seabird with strikingly bright blue feet. It lives on the Pacific coast of the Americas and is especially well known on the Galápagos Islands. Its feet play an important part in its courtship dance.
wichtigste: The blue-footed booby has bright blue feet.
It lives on the Pacific coast of the Americas and on the Galápagos Islands.
It eats fish, which it catches from the air in a plunge dive.
In the courtship dance the male lifts his blue feet in turn.
The bluer the feet, the healthier the bird.

abschnitte.text: The **blue-footed booby** is a seabird, about as big as a duck, with long, pointed wings. It breeds on coasts and islands in the eastern **Pacific**, from Mexico to Peru. It is especially well known from the **Galápagos Islands**, which belong to Ecuador. The blue colour of the feet comes from pigments in its food, the fresh fish.

The blue-footed booby hunts by **plunge diving**. It flies over the sea, spots a shoal of fish and plunges head first into the water with its wings folded back. Under water it snaps up fish such as sardines. Sometimes several birds hunt together. On land, by contrast, it looks rather clumsy, and that is where its name “booby” comes from.

In its **courtship**, the male proudly shows his feet. He lifts first one foot and then the other and stretches his beak and wings into the air. The female pays attention to the colour: **the bluer the feet**, the healthier and better fed the bird. The birds simply lay their eggs on the ground, and both parents look after the young.

gewusst: Blue-footed boobies warm their eggs with their well-supplied feet.

teile.einleitung: A mountain is a raised part of the land that is clearly higher than its surroundings. Mountains exist on all continents and even under the sea. The highest of all is Mount Everest in the Himalayas.
wichtigste: A mountain is a clear elevation of the Earth’s surface.
The highest point of a mountain is called the summit.
The highest mountain in the world is Mount Everest at 8,849 metres.
Many mountains together form a mountain range, for example the Alps.
The Matterhorn near Zermatt is one of the best-known mountains in the world.
The higher you climb, the colder it gets and the thinner the air is.
Mountains mostly form through the movement of the Earth’s plates or through volcanoes.

abschnitte.text: A mountain is an elevation that rises clearly above the landscape. Smaller elevations are called **hills**. The highest point is called the **summit**, and the steep sides are called flanks or slopes. The lowest point between two summits is a saddle, over which a pass often leads.

The Earth’s crust is made of large **plates** that move a few centimetres every year. When two plates collide, the rock is pushed together and folded, which is how the Alps and the Himalayas formed. Other mountains are **volcanoes**, built from cooled lava, like Kilimanjaro in Africa. At the same time, wind, water and ice slowly wear the mountains down again.

**Mount Everest** on the border of Nepal and China is the highest mountain on Earth at 8,849 metres. The highest mountain in Africa is Kilimanjaro, and the highest in South America is Aconcagua in the Andes. In Europe, Mont Blanc on the border between France and Italy is the highest peak in the Alps. Mauna Kea in Hawaii, measured from the sea floor, is even over 10,000 metres high.

Switzerland is a mountainous country, and around two thirds of its area lies in the Alps and the Jura. The highest Swiss summit is the **Dufourspitze** in the Monte Rosa massif at 4,634 metres. The **Matterhorn** near Zermatt is 4,478 metres high and world-famous for its pyramid shape. The Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau in the Bernese Oberland also attract people from all over the world.

For every 100 metres of height, it gets about 0.6 degrees colder on average. That is why no trees grow higher up. The limit is called the **tree line** and lies in the Alps at about 2,000 metres. Above it live animals such as the ibex, the chamois and the marmot. On the highest summits there is snow and ice all year round.

Mountains are important for water, wood and tourism. Many rivers rise in the mountains, because a lot of rain and snow falls there. Mountaineering, hiking and skiing are popular sports. But you have to be careful, because avalanches, rockfalls and thunderstorms can be dangerous.

begriffe.erklaerung: The highest point of a mountain.
Many mountains that together form a large chain of mountains.
The height above which trees can no longer grow.
Huge pieces of the Earth’s crust that move slowly.

gewusst: The Himalayas are still growing today by a few millimetres a year.
On the summit of Mount Everest the air has only about a third as much oxygen as at sea level.
The Matterhorn was first climbed in 1865 by Edward Whymper and his rope team.

teile.einleitung: Internal migration means that people move within their own country. For example they move from the village to the city or from the city to the suburbs. Such movements change whole regions.
wichtigste: Rural exodus is the movement from the countryside to the cities.
Suburbanisation means people move from the inner city to the surrounding area.
Reurbanisation means the inner cities grow again.
In stepwise migration, people move gradually to the big city.
In the USA, in the “Great Migration”, millions of African Americans moved from the South to the North and West.
In remote Swiss mountain valleys, emigration leads to an ageing population.

abschnitte.titel: From the countryside to the city
abschnitte.text: If there are no jobs, schools and shops in the countryside, many people move to the cities. This is called **rural exodus**. In many countries it is an important reason for **urbanisation**. Often people do not move directly to the big city but first to smaller places. This gradual movement is called **stepwise migration**.

abschnitte.titel: City, urban area and mountain regions
abschnitte.text: If people move from the inner city to the suburbs, for example because of cheaper flats or more greenery, this is called **suburbanisation**. In Switzerland many **urban-area municipalities** grew strongly in this way. Later more people moved back into the inner cities because of short distances and the cultural offer. This is called **reurbanisation**, and the city of Zurich has been growing again in this way since around 2000. From remote **mountain valleys**, by contrast, many young people move away. Mainly older people stay behind, and schools, village shops and post offices lose their customers.

Between about 1910 and 1970, around six million **African Americans** left the Southern states. They fled **racial segregation** and looked for industrial work in cities such as Chicago or Detroit. This movement is called the **Great Migration**. In the 1930s drought and wrong ways of working the soil in the Great Plains led to huge dust storms, the **Dust Bowl**. Hundreds of thousands of impoverished farming families therefore moved to California.

After **reunification** in 1990, mainly young people in Germany moved from east to west, because there were better jobs there. Many East German regions lost inhabitants and aged quickly. In **Indonesia**, the state resettled people from the densely populated island of Java to other islands with the **Transmigrasi** programme. This was meant to relieve Java. But the programme also led to conflicts and to forest clearing.

gewusst: The movement from the countryside to the city has led to more than half of all people living in cities today.

teile.einleitung: Camanchaca is the name of the dense coastal fog on the coast of the Atacama in Chile and Peru. It brings almost no rain, but a lot of moisture. People use fog nets to collect water from it.
wichtigste: Camanchaca is the coastal fog of the Atacama.
The Atacama is one of the driest deserts in the world.
The fog forms over the cold water of the Humboldt Current.
Fine fog nets catch droplets of water.
The water drips into channels and is collected.

abschnitte.text: The **Atacama** in northern Chile is one of the **driest deserts** in the world. In some places it hardly rains for years. Even so, it is often damp on the coast. Off the coast flows the cold **Humboldt Current**. Over the cool water, dense fog forms, which the wind drives onto the coast and the slopes. This fog is called **camanchaca**.

People on the coast use the fog with **fog nets**. These are large, fine nets stretched between posts. The tiny **droplets of water** in the fog cling to the threads. They run together and drip into **channels**. From there the water flows into tanks. In this way drinking water or water for gardens can be collected, without any electricity.

On the slopes that the fog reaches, special **plants** grow. They take their water directly from the damp air. In Peru, such green fog zones are called **lomas**. Animals such as insects also use the moisture. Without the camanchaca, there would be almost no life in these places.

gewusst: Fog nets are now also used in other dry countries, for example in Morocco.
Some desert beetles collect fog water on their backs.

teile.einleitung: The Atlantic Ocean, the Atlantic for short, is the great sea between Europe and Africa on one side and the Americas on the other. It is the second-largest ocean on Earth and reaches from the Arctic Ocean to Antarctica. Explorers sailed across it, and currents flow through it that even influence our weather in Europe.
wichtigste: The Atlantic Ocean is the second-largest ocean on Earth.
It lies between Europe and Africa in the east and the Americas in the west.
The warm ocean current called the Gulf Stream provides a mild climate in Western Europe.
Through the middle of the Atlantic runs a long mountain range under water, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Iceland lies right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
The Azores are a group of islands in the middle of the Atlantic that belongs to Portugal.
The water of the Rhine from Switzerland also reaches the Atlantic via the North Sea.

abschnitte.text: The Atlantic stretches like a great S between the continents of the Americas, Europe and Africa. With its **marginal seas** it covers about 106 million square kilometres, and only the Pacific is larger. The marginal seas include, for example, the North Sea, the Mediterranean and the Caribbean. Its deepest point lies in the **Puerto Rico Trench** at a good 8,300 metres.

On the sea floor the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge** runs from north to south, a huge mountain range under water. Here two tectonic plates are slowly drifting apart, by a few centimetres every year. That is why the Atlantic is constantly getting a little bit wider. Where the ridge rises out of the sea lie islands such as **Iceland** and the **Azores** with many volcanoes.

The **Gulf Stream** brings warm water from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic to Europe. As a result it is much milder in Western Europe than in regions at the same latitude, for example in Canada. In Norway, many ports therefore do not freeze over even in winter. In summer and autumn **hurricanes**, dangerous tropical storms, often form over the warm tropical Atlantic.

As early as the year 1000, Vikings sailed via Iceland and Greenland as far as North America. In 1492 Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic and reached the Caribbean. Later millions of emigrants, including from Switzerland, travelled by ship to America. In 1912 the **Titanic** sank after colliding with an iceberg in the North Atlantic, and in 1927 Charles Lindbergh became the first to fly alone non-stop across the ocean.

In the Atlantic live whales, dolphins, sharks and many kinds of fish such as cod, herring and tuna. Fishing is very important for countries such as Iceland, Norway and Portugal. In the **Sargasso Sea** west of the Azores float great mats of brown algae. The **eels** from Europe also travel there to reproduce.

Switzerland lies far from the sea, but the weather often comes from the Atlantic. Westerly winds bring moist air from the ocean, which falls here as rain or snow. The Rhine carries water from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea, a marginal sea of the Atlantic. And the young eels that grow up in Swiss waters were born in the Sargasso Sea in the middle of the Atlantic.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge sea between continents.
A great stream of water that moves through the sea like a river.
A long mountain range on the floor of the Atlantic where two tectonic plates drift apart.
A sea that belongs to an ocean but is partly surrounded by land.
A very strong tropical storm over the Atlantic.

gewusst: The name Atlantic comes from the Titan Atlas in Greek legend.
In Iceland you can walk or dive through a gap between two tectonic plates at one place.
European eels swim thousands of kilometres to the Sargasso Sea to spawn there.

teile.einleitung: China is a huge country in East Asia with a very ancient culture. Important things such as paper were invented here, and today over 1.4 billion people live in China.
wichtigste: The capital of China is Beijing.
The flag is red with five yellow stars.
At over 6,000 kilometres, the Yangtze is the longest river in China and in Asia.
Paper was invented in China about 2,000 years ago.
The official language is Standard Chinese, also called Mandarin.
In 2023, India overtook China as the most populous country.

abschnitte.text: China is one of the largest countries on Earth. The capital is **Beijing**. The **flag** is red, with one large and four small **yellow stars** in the top left corner. Since 1949 the country has been called the People’s Republic of China. In 2023, **India** overtook China as the most populous country, according to United Nations estimates, and both have over 1.4 billion inhabitants.

The **Yangtze** is the longest river in China and in all of Asia, and it is over 6,000 kilometres long. Another great river is the Yellow River. In the west there are high mountains and deserts, and in the east fertile plains and big cities. The **giant panda** lives in the mountain forests.

Most people speak **Chinese**. The official language is **Standard Chinese**, also called **Mandarin**, and it is taught in schools across the country. There are also many other Chinese languages and dialects. Writing uses thousands of **characters** rather than letters.

About 2,000 years ago, **paper** was invented in China. It later reached Europe by way of Arabia. The compass, gunpowder and printing with wooden blocks also come from China. Near **Xi’an**, farmers digging a well in 1974 discovered the **Terracotta Army**, thousands of life-size clay soldiers at the tomb of the first emperor.

The most important festival is the **Chinese New Year**, also called the Spring Festival. It takes place in January or February. There are fireworks, red lanterns and **dragon dances**. People often eat with two thin **chopsticks** made of wood, bamboo or plastic.

gewusst: The Great Wall of China is the longest structure in the world.
Chinese New Year falls on a different date every year because it follows the moon.

teile.einleitung: The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, ALMA for short, is a huge telescope array in the Atacama Desert in Chile. It consists of 66 antennas at a height of around 5,000 metres. Several countries run it together, including the member states of ESO such as Switzerland.
wichtigste: ALMA stands on the Chajnantor Plateau at a height of around 5,000 metres.
The array has 66 antennas.
It picks up radiation in millimetre and submillimetre waves.
Europe takes part through ESO, to which Switzerland also belongs.
Other partners are North America, East Asia and the host country Chile.

abschnitte.text: ALMA stands on the **Chajnantor Plateau** in northern Chile, at around **5,000 metres**. The array consists of **66 antennas** that look like large satellite dishes. Most have a diameter of 12 metres. The antennas work together like a single huge telescope. Special vehicles can move them to different places, so that the array can take finer or coarser images.

ALMA does not observe ordinary light but **millimetre and submillimetre waves**. This radiation comes from very cold gas and dust in space. In this way ALMA can show where new **stars** and **planets** are forming. Famous is an image of a dust disc around a young star in which you can see gaps where planets may be forming.

Water vapour in the air swallows the radiation that ALMA wants to measure. The plateau in the **Atacama** is extremely dry and lies above a large part of the atmosphere. That is why the place is ideal. For people, though, the thin air is tiring. Most staff therefore work in a building further down, and the antennas are controlled from there.

ALMA is a project of partners from **Europe**, **North America** and **East Asia** together with the host country **Chile**. Europe takes part through the European Southern Observatory **ESO**. **Switzerland** also belongs to it. The array has been in operation since the early 2010s and is among the largest ground-based telescopes in the world.

gewusst: ALMA was part of the network that showed the first picture of a black hole in 2019.
“Alma” is also a Spanish word and means “soul”.

teile.einleitung: The Caño Cristales is a small river in Colombia that glows in many colours at certain times. Because of its red, yellow and green tones, it is called the “river of five colours”.
wichtigste: The Caño Cristales lies in Colombia in South America.
It flows in the mountain region of the Serranía de la Macarena.
Water plants on the bed turn it a bright red at times.
Added to this are yellow, green and dark tones from sand, algae and rock.
The river is most colourful from about July to November.

abschnitte.text: The Caño Cristales has very **clear water**. This means you can see right down to the stony bed. Special **water plants** grow there that turn a strong red in the sun. Together with yellow sand, green algae and dark rock, they create a play of colours that recalls a rainbow.

The colours are not equally strong all year round. In the **rainy season**, the river has enough water, and the plants grow well. It glows most beautifully **from about July to November**. In the dry season the water level is low, and the plants rest.

The river lies in a **nature reserve**. Visitors may only visit it on certain paths and usually with a guide. This is to protect the delicate plants. The area was hard to reach for a long time, but more visitors come every year now.

gewusst: The red colour does not come from stones but from living plants in the water.
The Caño Cristales is often described as one of the most beautiful rivers in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Brahmaputra is one of the great rivers of Asia. It rises in Tibet, flows through India and Bangladesh and flows into the Bay of Bengal. On the way it has several names.
wichtigste: The Brahmaputra rises in Tibet, where it is called the Yarlung Tsangpo.
It breaks through the Himalayas in one of the deepest gorges on Earth.
In India it flows through a broad valley in the state of Assam.
In Bangladesh it is called the Jamuna and joins the Ganges.
In the river lies Majuli, one of the largest river islands in the world.
On its bank lies Kaziranga National Park, with many Indian rhinoceroses.

abschnitte.text: The Brahmaputra rises in the highlands of **Tibet**, north of the Himalayas. There it is called the **Yarlung Tsangpo** and flows from west to east for a long way. At the eastern end of the **Himalayas** it makes a great bend. In doing so it has cut an enormous **gorge**, which is regarded as one of the deepest on Earth. After that it flows south towards India.

In India the Brahmaputra flows through the state of **Assam** in the north-east. Here its valley is very wide, and the river often splits into many channels. Assam is famous for its **tea**, which grows on large plantations. In the river lies **Majuli**, one of the largest river islands in the world. Because of **erosion**, that is, the wearing away of land by water, it is getting smaller and smaller.

On the bank of the Brahmaputra lies **Kaziranga National Park**. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The largest population of **Indian rhinoceroses** in the world lives here. The Indian rhinoceros has only one horn and thick skin that looks like armour. Elephants, water buffalo and tigers also live in the park.

After India, the Brahmaputra flows into **Bangladesh**, where it is called the **Jamuna**. There it joins the **Ganges**. Together the rivers form a huge **delta** on the **Bay of Bengal**. In the rainy season, the **monsoon**, the river carries an enormous amount of water. Floods then often occur, but they also bring fertile mud to the fields.

gewusst: The name Brahmaputra means “son of Brahma”, after a god in Hinduism.
The Brahmaputra flows through three countries: China (Tibet), India and Bangladesh.

teile.einleitung: The Beagle conflict was a border dispute between Chile and Argentina. It was about three small islands at the very south of South America, near Tierra del Fuego. In 1978 it even threatened to lead to war.
wichtigste: The dispute was about the islands Picton, Lennox and Nueva.
The islands lie at the eastern end of the Beagle Channel near Tierra del Fuego.
In 1978 Chile and Argentina were close to war.
Pope John Paul II mediated between the two countries.
In 1984 Chile and Argentina signed a peace treaty.

abschnitte.text: The **Beagle Channel** is a strait at the far south of South America. It is named after the British research ship **HMS Beagle**, which surveyed the area in the 19th century. At its eastern end lie the islands **Picton, Lennox and Nueva**. Both countries wanted to own them. What mattered was not only the land but also the sea around it, with its fishing grounds and access to the Atlantic.

The two countries had the dispute examined by an **arbitration court**. In 1977 it awarded the islands to Chile. Argentina rejected the decision. At the end of 1978 both countries sent soldiers and warships to the region. At that time Chile and Argentina were both ruled by military governments. War seemed only a matter of days away.

At the last moment **Pope John Paul II** offered his help. He sent a cardinal as a **mediator**, that is, a neutral person who helps both sides find a solution. The negotiations lasted several years. In 1984 Chile and Argentina signed a **treaty of peace and friendship** in the Vatican. The islands went to Chile, and in return Argentina received more rights at sea.

gewusst: In Argentina the population voted on the treaty in a referendum in 1984, and a large majority said yes.
The young naturalist Charles Darwin also travelled around the world on HMS Beagle.

teile.einleitung: Comodoro Rivadavia is a port city on the Atlantic coast of Patagonia in Argentina. The Argentine oil industry began here in 1907, and it happened by chance.
wichtigste: Comodoro Rivadavia lies in the province of Chubut in Patagonia.
The city lies on the Atlantic, on the Gulf of San Jorge.
In 1907 people were looking for drinking water here and found oil.
This was the start of the Argentine oil industry.
The city became the centre of oil production in the country.

abschnitte.text: In the dry area, **drinking water** was short. So in 1907 people drilled for water. Instead of water, however, the drill struck **oil**. This chance event was the start of the **Argentine oil industry**.

After the discovery, Comodoro Rivadavia grew quickly. Many people moved here to work in **oil production**. The city became the most important **centre** of oil extraction in Argentina. Oil still shapes its economy today.

Patagonia is known for its **strong wind**. Near Comodoro Rivadavia there are therefore also **wind turbines** that generate electricity. The city lies between the sea and dry hills. It is named after a commodore, that is, a naval officer, called Martín Rivadavia.

gewusst: The Argentine oil industry owes its beginning to a failed search for water.

teile.einleitung: An archipelago is a group of islands lying close together in the sea. Some countries consist entirely of such island groups. In Europe too there are many well-known archipelagos, and even in a Swiss lake there is a small group of islands.
wichtigste: An archipelago is a group of islands.
A country that consists only of islands is called an island state.
Japan consists of four large main islands and many small islands.
The Azores belong to Portugal, the Canaries and the Balearics to Spain.
The Cyclades belong to Greece, the Faroe Islands to Denmark.
In Lake Maggiore lie the Brissago Islands.

abschnitte.text: An **archipelago** is a group of islands lying close together. The word came into German from Italian. Originally it meant the Aegean, the sea between Greece and Turkey with its many islands. Archipelagos form in various ways: through **volcanoes**, through corals or because parts of a mainland were flooded by the sea.

A country that lies entirely on islands is called an **island state**. **Japan** consists of four large main islands: Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku, plus thousands of small islands. **New Zealand** has a North Island and a South Island. Indonesia and the Philippines even consist of thousands of islands. Switzerland, by contrast, is a **landlocked country** with no sea.

In the Mediterranean lie the **Balearic Islands**. The largest island is **Majorca**, and they belong to Spain. Also belonging to Spain are the **Canary Islands** in the Atlantic off Africa. The **Azores** lie in the middle of the Atlantic and belong to Portugal. In the Aegean lie the **Cyclades** with well-known islands such as Naxos and Santorini. They belong to Greece.

The **Faroe Islands** lie in the North Atlantic between Scotland and Iceland. They belong to the Kingdom of **Denmark** but manage much for themselves. The islands are steep, green and almost without trees. Many seabirds breed on their cliffs. Off the coasts of Scotland, Norway and Sweden there are also large island groups.

Switzerland also has a small group of islands: the **Brissago Islands** in **Lake Maggiore**. There are two small islands. On the larger one there is a **botanical garden** with plants from all over the world. Thanks to the mild climate, even plants from warmer regions grow there. You reach the islands by boat.

gewusst: Indonesia is the largest island state in the world and consists of over 17,000 islands.
The Hawaiian Islands were formed by volcanoes in the middle of the Pacific.

teile.einleitung: A biodiversity hotspot is an area with especially many plant and animal species that exist only there. At the same time it is under heavy threat. Worldwide there are 36 such hotspots.
wichtigste: The term was coined by the British researcher Norman Myers in 1988.
A hotspot needs at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species.
It must have lost at least 70 per cent of its original vegetation.
Conservation International designates 36 hotspots (as of 2025).
They cover only around 2.4 per cent of the land area.
Even so, around half of all plant species occur only there.

abschnitte.text: **Biodiversity** means the variety of life. In 1988 the British environmental researcher **Norman Myers** described areas with especially many threatened species that occur only there. He called them **hotspots**, that is, “hot spots”. The conservation organisation **Conservation International** developed the concept further. It helps to decide where nature conservation is especially urgent.

A species is **endemic** if it occurs only in a certain, limited area, for example on an island or in a mountain range. If its habitat disappears, it dies out worldwide. A hotspot needs at least **1,500 endemic vascular plant species**, which is more than 0.5 per cent of all the world’s plant species. In addition, at least **70 per cent** of its original habitats must already be destroyed.

Conservation International designates **36 hotspots** worldwide. The latest, added in 2016, was the North American Coastal Plain. One example is the **Atlantic Forest** on the coast of Brazil, called Mata Atlântica in Portuguese. It was once huge, but today only a small part is left. Other hotspots are the **Caucasus** between Europe and Asia and the island of **Madagascar**.

There is also a hotspot near Switzerland: the **Mediterranean Basin**. Very many plant species grow there that exist nowhere else. At the same time, a large part of the original vegetation has been destroyed by farming, settlements and tourism. All the hotspots together cover only around **2.4 per cent** of the Earth’s land area. Even so, about **half of all plant species** occur only there.

gewusst: On Madagascar live the lemurs, a group of animals found in the wild nowhere else in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Atlas Mountains lie in the north-west of Africa, not far from Europe at all. They have high mountains, forests, villages and even snow in winter. South of them begins the largest hot desert in the world, the Sahara.
wichtigste: The Atlas Mountains lie in the north-west of Africa.
The highest mountain is Toubkal in Morocco, over 4,100 metres high.
South of the range lies the Sahara.
The city of Marrakesh lies close to the High Atlas.
Barbary macaques live in the forests.
The Berbers, who call themselves Amazigh, have lived here for a very long time.

abschnitte.text: The Atlas Mountains run through **Morocco**, **Algeria** and **Tunisia**. The highest mountain is called **Toubkal** and stands in Morocco. It is over 4,100 metres high and so higher than most Swiss mountains. Many hikers climb it in summer. In winter the high peaks are often white, because up there it is cold enough for **snow**.

To the north of the range lies the coast on the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. There it rains more, and fields and forests grow. To the south the **Sahara** begins. So the range separates two very different landscapes. It holds back the moist air from the sea, which is why it is so dry behind it.

At the foot of the High Atlas lies the city of **Marrakesh**. It is famous for the great square **Djemaa el Fna**. There is a colourful market there every day with food stalls, musicians and storytellers. From the city you can see the snow-covered mountains on clear days.

In the mountain forests live the **Barbary macaques**. They have thick fur and almost no tail. In the mountains the **Berbers** have lived for a very long time. They call themselves **Amazigh** and have a language of their own. Many live in villages of mud brick on the mountain slopes and keep sheep and goats.

gewusst: The range is named after Atlas, a giant from the old Greek legends who was said to carry the sky on his shoulders.
Barbary macaques belong to the macaques and are the only wild monkeys in Africa north of the Sahara.

teile.einleitung: The Beaufort scale shows how strongly the wind is blowing. It divides wind into 13 levels, from 0 for calm to 12 for hurricane. You recognise the levels by what the wind does.
wichtigste: The Beaufort scale measures wind force.
It was developed by the British admiral Francis Beaufort.
The scale runs from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane).
A hurricane has wind speeds from about 118 km/h.
The levels describe what the wind does on land or at sea.
Weather services and sailors still use the scale today.

abschnitte.text: The British naval officer **Francis Beaufort** developed the scale at the beginning of the 19th century. At that time there were still no good instruments for measuring wind. So Beaufort described how a sailing ship behaves at which wind. This way sailors could judge the wind the same way everywhere. Later the scale was adapted to waves and to observations on land.

At **force 0** it is calm, and smoke rises straight up. At force 3 leaves and thin twigs move constantly. At force 6 the wind whistles and you have trouble with an umbrella. From **force 8** people speak of a gale, from force 9 of a **storm**. Walking is then difficult, and branches break off.

The highest level is **force 12**, the **hurricane**. The wind is then at least about 118 km/h. A hurricane can uproot trees, tear off roofs and cause great damage. Force 11 is called a “violent storm”. At sea, huge waves pile up in a hurricane, and the air is full of spray.

Switzerland also experiences strong storms. Well known is **Hurricane Lothar** of December 1999, which caused huge damage in many forests. In the Alps, the **foehn**, a warm downslope wind, can also reach storm force. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss today usually give wind speed in km/h. But the Beaufort levels help you understand the effect quickly.

gewusst: The Beaufort Sea in the Arctic Ocean is named after Francis Beaufort.
For very strong cyclones, some countries have extended the scale beyond level 12.

teile.einleitung: Badlands are landscapes in which rain and water have cut deeply into soft layers of rock. Hardly any plants grow, but there are gullies, ridges and colourful rock walls. The best-known badlands lie in South Dakota in the USA.
wichtigste: Badlands are heavily dissected, almost bare erosion landscapes.
They form where rain quickly wears away soft layers of sediment and ash.
The most famous badlands lie in South Dakota.
There is Badlands National Park there.
Many fossils can be found in the rock layers.

abschnitte.text: Badlands form in rather dry regions with **soft rock**, for example clay, sand or volcanic ash. It rains rarely, but when it does, it is often heavy. The running water quickly carries off the loose material. Because hardly any plants grow, nothing holds the ground in place. This creates deep **gullies**, sharp **ridges** and little towers. This wearing away is called **erosion**.

In **South Dakota** lies **Badlands National Park**. Its rock walls show many coloured stripes in red, yellow, grey and white. Each layer was laid down at a different time. In these layers researchers have found many **fossils** of prehistoric mammals. Today bison, prairie dogs and bighorn sheep live in the park.

The **Lakota**, a people of the Native Americans, called the area “bad land”. French fur traders also described it as land that was hard to cross. From this came the English name **badlands**. Today experts use the term for all similar landscapes in the world.

gewusst: The badlands change comparatively fast, because every year part of the soft rock is worn away.

teile.einleitung: The Great Wall of China is the longest structure in the world. Over many centuries, Chinese emperors had it built to protect their empire from attackers from the north.
wichtigste: The wall was meant to protect China from horse-riding peoples from the north.
With all its sections it is over 21,000 kilometres long.
Around 220 BC, Emperor Qin Shihuangdi had older stretches of wall joined up.
Most of the well-preserved parts date from the Ming dynasty.
The wall cannot be seen from the Moon with the naked eye.
Today millions of people walk along the wall every year.

abschnitte.text: Nomadic **horse-riding peoples** such as the Xiongnu and later the Mongols attacked China again and again from the **north**. The wall was meant to make these attacks more difficult. Soldiers guarded it. At intervals along the wall stand **watchtowers**, from which enemies could be spotted early and signals given with smoke.

Individual states built defensive walls early on. Around 220 BC, **Qin Shihuangdi**, the first emperor of a united China, had these stretches of wall joined up. Many more emperors later added to it. The best-known parts were built under the **Ming dynasty** (1368 to 1644) and are about 500 years old.

Older sections are made of **rammed earth**. The emperors of the Ming dynasty had the wall greatly strengthened with **stones** and fired **bricks**. The wall runs over mountains, through valleys and across deserts. Some sections are very steep and have many steps.

A survey in 2012 arrived at over **21,000 kilometres** with all the sections. The wall is only a few metres wide, though. So it is not true that you can see it **from the Moon** with the naked eye. That is a widespread mistake.

Today the wall is a major **sight**. Every year millions of people walk along it, especially near Beijing. Since 1987 it has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. In 2007 it was chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

gewusst: The Great Wall is really not a single wall but many walls from different periods.
At over 21,000 kilometres, it would be longer than half the way around the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Angkor is a huge ruined city in the north-west of Cambodia. From the 9th to the 15th century it was the centre of the Khmer Empire. Today its temples are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and attract visitors from all over the world.
wichtigste: Angkor lies in the north-west of Cambodia, near the town of Siem Reap.
From the 9th to the 15th century Angkor was the capital of the Khmer Empire.
Angkor was one of the largest cities of its time.
The best-known temple is Angkor Wat, which is shown on the flag of Cambodia.
In the royal city of Angkor Thom stands the Bayon with its stone faces.
Lake Tonle Sap supplied fish and water.
The Frenchman Henri Mouhot made Angkor known in Europe around 1860.

abschnitte.text: The **Khmer** are the people who today make up the majority in Cambodia. From the **9th to the 15th century** their kings ruled a large empire in South-East Asia. Angkor was their capital. Here the kings had numerous temples built of stone. The dwelling houses were of wood and have long since disappeared. Angkor was one of the **largest cities** of its time.

**Angkor Thom** means “great city”. King Jayavarman VII had it surrounded with a wall and large gates around 1200. In its middle stands the temple **Bayon**. It is famous for over 200 huge, smiling **stone faces** on its towers. Exactly whom they represent is not entirely certain.

Nearby lies **Tonle Sap**, the largest lake in South-East Asia. It supplied the people with fish and water. The Khmer built an ingenious system of **canals** and huge water basins. In this way they could store water for the dry season and grow a lot of **rice**. That made it possible to feed very many people.

After the 15th century Angkor lost importance, and the jungle overgrew many temples. But Angkor was never entirely forgotten in Cambodia, and monks went on living there. In Europe the city became known through the French explorer **Henri Mouhot**. His travel reports with drawings appeared after his death and aroused great interest.

The best-known temple is **Angkor Wat**. It is so important for Cambodia that it appears on the country’s **flag**. Hardly any other country shows a building on its flag. Since 1992 Angkor has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Many countries help to preserve the old temples.

gewusst: With laser scans from aircraft, researchers have discovered traces of roads and canals beneath the forest of Angkor.
The temple complexes of Angkor extend over around 400 square kilometres.

teile.einleitung: The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth. It can grow to around 30 metres long and weigh over 100 tonnes. Even so, it eats mainly tiny crustaceans.
wichtigste: The blue whale is the largest animal of all time.
It grows to around 30 metres long and over 100 tonnes in weight.
It is a mammal and breathes with lungs.
Instead of teeth it has baleen plates, with which it sieves krill out of the water.
A baby blue whale is already around 7 metres long at birth.
In the past the blue whale was hunted heavily, but today it is protected.

abschnitte.text: Large **blue whales** grow to around **30 metres** long, about as long as two buses one behind the other. They weigh well over **100 tonnes**, as much as many elephants together. No dinosaur was so heavy. Blue whales live in all the great **oceans**. They often swim alone or in pairs and cover long distances.

The blue whale eats mainly **krill**. These are small crustaceans that live in huge swarms. The whale has no teeth but **baleen plates**: long plates of horn that hang down from the upper jaw. It takes an enormous mouthful of water with krill. Then it presses the water out through the baleen, and the krill stays behind as in a sieve.

Whales are **mammals**, not fish. They breathe air with their **lungs** and have to come to the surface for it. When breathing out, the blue whale blows warm, moist air upwards. This column is called the **blow** and can be around 9 metres high. The young drink milk from their mother. A newborn blue whale is already around **7 metres** long and weighs about as much as two cars.

In the 20th century very many blue whales were hunted by **whaling ships**. People wanted mainly their fat, the blubber oil. As a result blue whales were almost wiped out. Since the 1960s they have been **protected** worldwide. Since then the populations have been slowly recovering, but there are still far fewer blue whales than before. The species is still regarded as **endangered**.

gewusst: Blue whales are among the loudest animals in the world: their deep calls can be heard under water over very long distances.
A blue whale can eat several tonnes of krill in a day.

teile.einleitung: The Arabian Peninsula lies in Western Asia between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. It is the largest peninsula on Earth and consists mostly of desert. Here lie Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Oman, among others.
wichtigste: The Arabian Peninsula is the largest peninsula on Earth.
It covers around 3 million square kilometres, over seventy times Switzerland.
Saudi Arabia takes up the largest part.
In the south lies the Rub al-Khali, the largest continuous sand desert.
Yemen lies in the south-west, and Oman, with its capital Muscat, in the south-east.
A lot of drinking water is obtained from seawater.
The Strait of Hormuz is important for the transport of oil.

abschnitte.text: The Arabian Peninsula covers around **3 million square kilometres**. That makes it the **largest peninsula** on Earth and over seventy times as big as Switzerland. In the west lies the **Red Sea**, in the east the **Persian Gulf**. **Saudi Arabia** takes up the largest part. Added to that are Yemen, Oman, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Kuwait. The island state of Bahrain lies just off the coast.

A large part of the peninsula is **desert**. In the north lies the **Nefud** with its reddish sand dunes. In the south stretches the **Rub al-Khali**, the “Empty Quarter”. It is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth, about as big as France, and its dunes rise to over 200 metres. A **wadi** is a mostly dry river valley that carries water briefly only after rare rainfall.

On the peninsula it rains very little, and there are no permanently flowing rivers. That is why many states get their drinking water by **desalinating seawater**. In large plants the salt is removed from the seawater. This takes a lot of energy. In the past **oases** with springs and wells were the most important places to live.

**Yemen** lies in the south-west on the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Its mountains receive more rain, so there are terraced fields there. Yemen also includes the island of **Socotra** in the Indian Ocean. It is famous for its strange **dragon’s blood trees**, which look like umbrellas. **Oman** lies in the south-east, with its capital **Muscat** on the Gulf of Oman.

Beneath the peninsula lie huge reserves of **oil** and natural gas. They have made several states very rich. Between Oman and Iran lies the **Strait of Hormuz**. About a fifth of the oil traded worldwide is shipped through this strait. It connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman. For Islam the peninsula is important because **Mecca** and **Medina** lie here.

gewusst: On Socotra many plants grow that are found nowhere else in the world.
The Arabian Peninsula has not a single large river that carries water all year round.

teile.einleitung: A fault-block mountain range forms when the Earth’s crust breaks into large blocks. These blocks, called fault blocks, are raised, lowered or tilted. Well-known examples are the Black Forest, the Vosges and the Harz.
wichtigste: Fault-block mountains form when blocks of crust are raised or tilted along faults.
A raised block is called a horst, a lowered one a graben.
The Black Forest and the Vosges form the shoulders of the Upper Rhine Graben.
A block raised on one side only, like the Harz, is called a tilted block.
When the crust is stretched, normal faults form.
Basel lies at the southern end of the Upper Rhine Graben.

abschnitte.text: The outer layer of the Earth, the **Earth’s crust**, is not completely rigid. If it is stretched or squeezed, it can break along **faults**. A fault is a break surface along which blocks of rock move against each other. The individual blocks are called **fault blocks**. They can be raised, lowered or **tilted**. This is how a fault-block mountain range forms.

A block **raised** between faults is called a **horst**. It lies higher than its surroundings. A block that has **sunk** is called a **graben**. Both typically form when the crust is **stretched**. A block then slides down along a sloping surface, which is called a **normal fault**. If a block is strongly raised on one side only, it is called a **tilted block**, a bit like a writing desk. Examples are the **Harz** and the **Ore Mountains**.

Between Basel and Frankfurt lies the **Upper Rhine Graben**. As the graben sank, its edges were pushed up. To the east lies the **Black Forest**, and to the west the **Vosges**. The basement rock of the Black Forest is a remnant of the **Variscan mountains**, which formed about 300 million years ago in the **Carboniferous**. They were worn away and later raised again as a fault block.

**Basel** lies at the southern end of the Upper Rhine Graben. Here the crust is still moving today. In **1356**, a severe earthquake shook the city. It is regarded as the strongest historically recorded earthquake north of the Alps. Many buildings collapsed, and fires destroyed large parts of the city. That is why, to this day, people in the Basel region pay special attention to earthquake-proof building.

In the west of the USA, especially in **Nevada** and **Utah**, lies the **Basin and Range** region. There the crust is being stretched and breaks into many parallel blocks. Raised horsts form mountain ranges, and sunken grabens form basins. The **Sierra Nevada** in California is a tilted fault block: in the east it is steeply raised, and towards the west it slopes down gently.

gewusst: In some places the Upper Rhine Graben is filled with over 3,000 metres of deposits.
Because the crust is thin, the ground in the Upper Rhine Graben is warmer in some places than elsewhere.

teile.einleitung: An anemometer is an instrument for measuring wind speed. Weather services, airports and cable cars need such devices to know how strongly the wind is blowing. The name comes from the Greek word “anemos” for wind.
wichtigste: An anemometer measures how fast the wind is blowing.
Many anemometers have small cups that turn in the wind.
The faster the cups turn, the stronger the wind.
There are also anemometers that measure with ultrasound.
Wind speed is given in metres per second, kilometres per hour or knots.

abschnitte.text: The best-known form is the **cup anemometer**. It has three or four small hemispheres on arms that turn around an axis. The wind pushes harder into the open side of a cup than against the round side. That is why the cross turns. The faster it turns, the **stronger** the wind. A counter converts the turns into a speed.

There are also anemometers with a small **propeller** that turns in the wind. Modern devices often measure with **ultrasound**. They send sound waves back and forth between sensors. The wind changes how long the sound takes. From this the device calculates the strength and direction of the wind, without any moving parts at all.

Weather services such as **MeteoSwiss** measure the wind at many stations, including on mountain peaks. The device usually stands on a mast, about 10 metres above the ground. Airports need the measurements for safe take-offs and landings. Cable cars have to stop in a strong storm. **Wind turbines** also have anemometers built in.

gewusst: The first simple wind gauges were described in Europe as early as the 15th century.
Sailors often give wind strength in knots or on the Beaufort scale from 0 to 12.

teile.einleitung: Nigeria in West Africa is the most populous country in Africa. Its population is very young and growing fast. That brings opportunities but also great challenges.
wichtigste: Around 2024 Nigeria ranked sixth among the most populous countries in the world.
Over 40 per cent of people are younger than 15.
The median age is around 18 years.
Around 2023 the fertility rate was over 4 children per woman.
Over 500 languages are spoken in Nigeria.
Since 1991 Abuja has been the capital, and Lagos is the largest city.

abschnitte.text: After India, China, the USA, Indonesia and Pakistan, Nigeria came in **sixth place** among the most populous countries around 2024. No other country in Africa has so many people. The UN expects Nigeria to climb further in the ranking. The country is very diverse: **over 500 languages** are spoken. The official language is **English**, and Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo are also widespread.

In Nigeria **over 40 per cent** of people are children under 15. In Switzerland it is only around 15 per cent. The **median age** is around 18 years. That means half of the people are younger and the other half older. In Switzerland the median age is over 40 years. Around 2023 the **fertility rate** was over 4 children per woman. It is falling but is far above the replacement level.

The **demographic transition** describes how births and deaths in a country change with development. First the death rate falls, later the birth rate too. Nigeria is in the transition from the **second to the third phase**. The death rate has fallen clearly, while the birth rate is only slowly beginning to fall. That is why the population is still growing strongly.

In 1991 **Abuja** replaced Lagos as the capital. Abuja was built as a planned city in the middle of the country, partly so as not to favour any of the large ethnic groups. **Lagos** remained the largest city and the economic centre. There the city is growing so fast that slums are appearing, for example **Makoko**, whose houses stand on stilts in the lagoon. Every year Nigeria needs millions of new **jobs and school places**, as well as hospitals and homes.

gewusst: The residents of Makoko often move between their houses on the water by canoe.
Nigeria’s film industry, called “Nollywood”, is among the largest in the world measured by the number of films.

teile.einleitung: In mountaineering, people climb high mountains. It is exciting but also dangerous. That is why it takes good equipment, a lot of knowledge and sometimes a mountain guide.
wichtigste: With crampons under your boots you do not slip on ice.
A helmet protects against falling stones.
With a rope, mountaineers secure each other.
In mountain huts you can eat and sleep.
In a thunderstorm you should leave summits and ridges quickly.
In 1978 Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler climbed Everest without oxygen bottles.
In 1956 a Swiss team stood on Mount Everest for the first time.

abschnitte.text: Mountaineers need good boots and warm clothes. On glaciers and ice they wear **crampons**, which are metal spikes under the boots. They dig into the ice and give a grip. A **helmet** protects the head from falling stones. With a strong **rope**, mountaineers tie themselves to each other. If one slips, the others hold him.

High in the mountains stand **mountain huts**. There mountaineers can eat, sleep and rest. In Switzerland the **Swiss Alpine Club SAC** runs over 150 such huts. On very high mountains such as in the Himalayas there are no huts. There, expeditions set up a **base camp** at the foot of the mountain, a large tent camp. From there they set off for the summit.

On the mountain the **weather** can change quickly. If a thunderstorm comes, you should leave summits and ridges at once, because lightning often strikes high points. Other dangers are **rockfall**, avalanches and crevasses. At great height the air is thin, and you get less oxygen. **Mountain guides** know the routes, the weather and the dangers. In Switzerland they undergo long training for this.

In 1865 a group around the Englishman Edward Whymper climbed the **Matterhorn** for the first time. In 1953 Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first to stand on **Mount Everest**, the highest mountain in the world. In 1956 members of a **Swiss expedition** reached the summit, the second successful ascent ever. In 1978 **Reinhold Messner** from South Tyrol and Peter Habeler were the first to climb Everest without oxygen from bottles.

gewusst: The same Swiss expedition of 1956 also achieved the first ascent of Lhotse, the fourth highest mountain in the world.
The Swiss Alpine Club SAC was founded as early as 1863.

teile.einleitung: The exclusive economic zone, EEZ for short, is an area of sea off the coast of a state. There only that coastal state may fish and use mineral resources. It reaches up to 200 nautical miles out to sea.
wichtigste: The exclusive economic zone reaches up to 200 nautical miles from the coast.
That is around 370 kilometres.
It is regulated in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Fish, oil, natural gas and other mineral resources there belong to the coastal state.
Ships of other states may still sail through the zone.

abschnitte.text: Directly on the coast lies the **territorial sea**, which reaches 12 nautical miles and is treated almost like state territory. The **exclusive economic zone** adjoins it. It reaches up to 200 nautical miles, that is around 370 kilometres, from the coast. A **nautical mile** measures 1,852 metres. If two countries lie closer together, they have to negotiate the border between their zones.

abschnitte.titel: What the coastal state may do
abschnitte.text: In its economic zone the coastal state alone decides on **fishing**. **Oil**, **natural gas** and other resources in the sea floor also belong to it. It may, for example, build wind farms there and protect the marine environment. Other states keep important rights, however: their ships may pass through, aircraft may fly over, and cables and pipelines may be laid.

The rules are set out in the **United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea** of 1982. A great many states have signed it. Landlocked countries such as Switzerland are affected too, because ocean-going ships sail under the Swiss flag. For them it is important that freedom of navigation also applies in foreign economic zones.

gewusst: States with many small islands spread widely across the ocean often have huge economic zones, much larger than their land.

teile.einleitung: The Cueva de las Manos is a cave in Argentina. Its name means “Cave of the Hands”. On its rock walls you can see hundreds of coloured handprints that are thousands of years old.
wichtigste: The Cueva de las Manos lies in the province of Santa Cruz in Patagonia, Argentina.
The name means “Cave of the Hands”.
The oldest pictures are about 9,000 years old.
Most of the prints show left hands.
Since 1999 the cave has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: In the cave and under the rock overhangs, very many **hand pictures** can be seen in red, yellow, white and black. Most are **negative prints**: people placed a hand against the wall and blew paint around it, probably through a small tube. This left the shape of the hand free of paint. Most of the hands are **left hands**, probably because the right hand held the tube.

The painters were **hunters and gatherers** who lived in Patagonia thousands of years ago. Besides the hands, the pictures also show **hunting scenes** with **guanacos**, wild relatives of the llama. People made the colours from earths and minerals. The oldest pictures are about 9,000 years old.

The cave lies in the canyon of the **Río Pinturas** in the province of **Santa Cruz**. The landscape there is dry, windy and almost deserted. Since **1999**, the Cueva de las Manos has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Visitors may only view the pictures with a guide and from a walkway, so that they are not damaged.

gewusst: “Río Pinturas” means “River of Paintings” in English.
There are so many hands on the walls that they often overlap like a colourful noticeboard.

teile.einleitung: The banana is one of the most popular fruits in the world. It grows in warm countries on large plants and is harvested green. By ship it travels across the sea to Swiss shops.
wichtigste: Bananas are harvested green and ripen only on the way and in storage.
Ripe bananas are yellow, and brown spots show they are very ripe.
The banana plant is not a tree but a giant herb.
Bananas grow in large bunches and often on plantations.
India harvests the most bananas, Ecuador exports the most (as of 2024).
As it ripens, starch is converted into sugar.

abschnitte.text: The banana plant looks like a tree but is a giant **herb**. Its trunk is made not of wood but of **rolled-up leaves** that fit tightly into each other. At the top grow large, long leaves. From the middle a flower stalk grows on which the fruits form. After harvesting the trunk dies, and a new shoot grows up from the ground.

Bananas grow in large **bunches** on a fruit stalk. One bunch can carry over a hundred bananas. Bananas are often grown on huge **plantations**. These are large fields on which only one kind of plant grows. The plants need a lot of warmth and water, which is why they grow in the **tropics** close to the equator.

Bananas are picked **green**. Then they travel in **refrigerated ships** across the Atlantic to Europe. The cool slows down ripening. In Europe they go into ripening rooms, where they slowly turn yellow. Many bananas in Swiss shops come from **Ecuador**, Colombia or Costa Rica.

As it ripens, the **starch** in the banana is converted into **sugar**. That is why a ripe banana tastes sweet and is soft. The skin turns from green to **yellow**. Brown spots show that the banana is very ripe. Bananas contain a lot of potassium and give quick energy, which is why athletes like to eat them.

**India** harvests the most bananas in the world (as of 2024). Almost all of them are eaten in the country itself, though. **Ecuador** in South America sells the most bananas abroad (as of 2024). For many countries in the tropics bananas are an important export product. In Switzerland there are also bananas with the **Fairtrade label**, for which farmers are supposed to receive fair prices.

gewusst: Botanically speaking, the banana is a berry.
The bananas in the shop have almost no hard seeds, whereas wild bananas are full of them.

teile.einleitung: Argentinosaurus was a huge dinosaur that lived around 95 million years ago. Its bones were discovered in the province of Neuquén in Patagonia. It is regarded as one of the largest land animals that ever existed.
wichtigste: Argentinosaurus was found in the province of Neuquén in Patagonia.
It lived in the Late Cretaceous, around 95 million years ago.
It was a plant eater with a long neck and a long tail.
It belongs to the titanosaurs, a group of sauropods.
Only a few of its bones are known, so its size and weight are estimates.

abschnitte.text: The name **Argentinosaurus** means “lizard from Argentina”. The first bones were found by a farmer in the 1980s in the province of **Neuquén** in Patagonia. Researchers described the species in 1993. Argentinosaurus lived in the **Late Cretaceous**, around 95 million years ago. It belongs to the **titanosaurs**, a group of large, long-necked sauropods.

Of Argentinosaurus only **a few bones** are known, such as vertebrae, ribs and a leg bone. A single back vertebra is bigger than a child. From these finds researchers estimate that it was about **30 to 35 metres** long. Its weight was probably many dozens of tonnes. Because the skeleton is incomplete, the estimates differ widely.

Argentinosaurus was a **plant eater**. With its long neck it reached leaves high up in the trees. It walked on four pillar-like legs. To grow so big, it had to eat huge amounts of plants every day. In Patagonia large predatory dinosaurs also lived at the same time.

gewusst: In a museum in Plaza Huincul in Argentina you can see bones of Argentinosaurus.
Titanosaurs laid eggs, and whole fields of fossilised titanosaur eggs have been found in Patagonia.

teile.einleitung: Bangkok is the capital of Thailand and the largest city in the country. It lies on the Chao Phraya River and is known for magnificent temples, floating markets and lively streets. The Thais themselves call their capital Krung Thep.
wichtigste: Bangkok is the capital of Thailand.
The city lies on the Chao Phraya River.
The Thais call it Krung Thep, “City of Angels”.
Well known are the floating markets, where traders sell from boats.
Wat Arun means “Temple of Dawn”.
In Wat Phra Kaeo the Emerald Buddha is worshipped.

abschnitte.text: Bangkok lies on the **Chao Phraya**, which flows through the middle of the city into the Gulf of Thailand. Many ferries, water taxis and barges ply on it. In the past Bangkok was criss-crossed by countless **canals**, called **khlongs**. Many of them were later filled in and made into streets. Since the end of the 18th century Bangkok has been the capital of the country.

The Thais call their capital **Krung Thep**, which means “City of Angels”. That is only the short form. The full name is one of the **longest place names in the world**. It lists many honorific titles of the city. The name Bangkok is used mainly by foreigners.

In Bangkok there are hundreds of Buddhist temples, called **wat** in Thai. **Wat Arun**, the “Temple of Dawn”, stands on the riverbank. Its tall tower is decorated with colourful pieces of porcelain. Next to the Royal Palace lies **Wat Phra Kaeo** with the **Emerald Buddha**, the most important Buddha statue in Thailand. It is made of green stone and is dressed anew by the king several times a year.

Bangkok and its surroundings are known for **floating markets**. There traders sell fruit, vegetables and hot food straight from their boats. Customers stand on the bank or pass by in a boat themselves. Besides these there are many **street kitchens** and night markets in the city. Street food is an important part of life in Bangkok.

Bangkok is a huge, lively city with a lot of traffic. Well known are the **tuk-tuks**, small three-wheeled taxis. To avoid the traffic jams, elevated trains and an underground also run through the city. It is hot all year round, and in the **rainy season** there are often heavy showers.

gewusst: In the temple of Wat Pho lies a huge gilded Buddha statue more than 40 metres long.
Bangkok lies only just above sea level and so is easily flooded.

teile.einleitung: A container ship is a large cargo ship that carries thousands of containers across the seas. Without container ships, our shops would have far fewer goods from distant countries.
wichtigste: Container ships carry large metal boxes full of goods.
The containers are mostly made of steel and are cuboid in shape.
All containers come in standard sizes.
In the port, huge cranes, the container gantry cranes, lift the containers off the ship.
The largest ships carry over 24,000 standard containers (as of 2025).
The world’s largest container shipping company, MSC, has its headquarters in Geneva (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: A **container ship** carries thousands of **containers**. Inside are goods such as clothes, toys, electronics or machines. The containers are **stacked** in the hull of the ship and high up on deck. Many of the things we buy have made a long journey on a container ship.
